whyItMatters: Today's throughline is governance and data — who controls information, and who's qualified to make the rules. Axios reporting that most lawmakers regulating AI don't actually use it lands squarely in your public-institution governance lane, and it pairs with the mortgage-industry debate over which facts an AI is allowed to treat as 'true' — both are really about accountability structures, which is exactly the frame you're productizing. On the higher-ed side, Canada's grad-student numbers are climbing even as the study-permit machinery gets more restrictive, a tension your enrollment clients feel directly. The Zillow arbitration ruling is a reminder that portal power and data-access rules are being litigated in real time, which matters for any brokerage strategy. And close to home, the Kamloops mayoral court fight and shelter-campus debate keep shaping the local backdrop as the municipal race heats up. Watch the EU-Canada associate-member proposal — it's a real signal about where Canadian trade and talent flows are heading.
audioScript:
Good morning, Midya. It's Wednesday, September sixteenth, twenty twenty-six. Today's news keeps circling one idea — governance, data, and who's actually qualified to make the rules — so let's dig into where that matters for your work.

Let's start with a story that lands right in the middle of your public-institution governance lane, because it's almost too on-the-nose. Axios interviewed more than two dozen lawmakers and governors and reported that many of them — particularly the older, more influential ones — don't use AI at all, or have barely touched it. And this is happening at the exact moment they're under enormous pressure to regulate it. Think about the contradiction there. You've got people being asked to write the guardrails for a technology that some of them can't describe, can't operate, and in a few cases openly dismiss. The critics quoted in the piece make the obvious point: it's very hard to grasp how fast something is moving, or what it might unleash, if you've never sat with it.

Now, why does this matter to you specifically? Because this is the perfect illustration of the credibility gap you keep running into when you advise public institutions. Boards, university leadership teams, senior administrators — a lot of them are in exactly the same position as those lawmakers. They're being asked to approve AI policy, sign off on vendor contracts, and set data-residency rules, and they've never once used the tools they're governing. That's not a knock on them; it's a structural reality. And it's precisely the wedge for your governance work. The content angle here writes itself: before a public board can responsibly write AI policy, it needs a baseline of literacy — not to become engineers, but to understand what they're authorizing. That's a thought-leadership piece with your name on it. The regulators-without-the-tool story is the hook; the fix — a literacy-before-policy framework for public governance — is your product.

Staying in the AI world, there's a really sharp piece from HousingWire that on the surface looks like a mortgage-industry story, but it's actually a governance story wearing a real-estate costume. The headline is: AI can read the mortgage file, but who decides which facts are true? Here's the situation. When an AI ingests a loan file, it's pulling from payroll data, the loan-origination system, tax records, and bank statements — and those sources conflict all the time. Different income figures. Different balances. So the hard problem isn't reading the documents, which AI does easily. The hard problem is adjudication: deciding when a piece of evidence counts as supported versus unresolved. Who gets to declare a fact true?

That's the exact question your real-estate clients — and your husband's brokerage world — should be asking about every AI tool a vendor pitches them. Everyone's selling speed. Faster document processing, faster underwriting, faster file review. But the value, and the risk, sits in the adjudication layer, not the reading layer. The content angle: AI in real estate operations needs a source-of-truth governance framework, because a tool that confidently resolves a conflict the wrong way is more dangerous than a slow human who flags it. That's a smart, defensible position you could publish, and it separates you from the hype crowd who just talk about time savings.

And one more to keep on your radar, quickly. Axios also reports the U.S. administration is escalating what they call a war on federal data — agencies changing how they collect and publish information, with politics increasingly baked into the process. I'm flagging it not because it's American politics, but because it's a live example of how fragile so-called neutral public data really is. When you're advising institutions on data residency and governance, the assumption that public datasets are stable and apolitical is worth questioning. Watch that trend line.

On the marketing side, Jersey Mike's has kicked off its NFL campaign, and Marketing Dive frames it as the brand's most integrated effort to date — its first major push since going public in July. The broader signal is the one worth holding onto: digital marketing spend is surging as brands chase integrated, measurable, cross-channel reach around tentpole moments like the NFL season. For your consulting practice, the interesting thread isn't the sandwiches — it's that a newly public company is using a big sports moment to define its brand story under investor scrutiny. That's the pressure your executive clients feel: the campaign has to build brand and prove ROI at the same time. It's a useful reference point when you're helping a client justify integrated spend to a skeptical board.

Now to higher education, where there's a genuinely interesting divergence today. The PIE News reports that the number of new international graduate students in Canada is soaring — climbing sharply even as the overall study-permit environment gets tighter and undergraduate volumes come under pressure. Sit with that split for a second, because it's strategically important. The headline narrative all year has been contraction: caps, cuts, falling enrolment, the kind of thing we've been tracking in Kamloops with TRU. But underneath that, the graduate segment is growing. That tells you demand isn't collapsing — it's redistributing. Master's and PhD pipelines are behaving very differently from the undergraduate market.

And that connects directly to the second higher-ed item. Canada's twenty twenty-six study-permit rules now exempt Master's and PhD applicants from the provincial attestation letter requirement, while raising proof-of-funds thresholds, with specific changes flagged for Indian applicants. Put the two stories together and the picture sharpens: Ottawa is deliberately steering the system toward higher-value graduate students while squeezing the undergraduate volume game. For any enrollment or recruitment client, that's the whole ballgame. The institutions that reposition toward graduate recruitment — and build the marketing and program infrastructure to support it — are going to be far better insulated than the ones still fighting over a shrinking undergraduate pool. That's a strategic conversation you should be having with anyone in this space.

The third higher-ed item is more of a values-and-governance story, but it's substantive. University Affairs covered a new Scholars at Risk report finding that attacks on higher education — erosion of institutional autonomy, political interference — are spreading globally, and crucially, into liberal democracies, including the United States. The report urges Canada not to assume it's immune, and to actively defend academic values and institutional independence. I flag it because your work sits at the intersection of higher ed and public governance, and the theme of institutional autonomy under pressure is going to keep surfacing. It's context that makes you smarter in the room, even if it's not a client deliverable.

On to real estate. The big industry item is a court ruling: a federal judge in Illinois denied Zillow's request for an injunction and sent the MRED claims — along with Zillow's claims against Compass — into arbitration. If you strip away the procedural language, this is another chapter in the long fight over who controls listing data and how much power the big portals get to wield. These portal-versus-brokerage battles matter because they shape the ground rules for how listings flow, how data gets shared, and ultimately how much leverage independent brokerages retain. For a brokerage strategy conversation, the takeaway is that the rules of the data game are still being actively litigated — nobody should assume today's arrangement is permanent.

The second real-estate item is quieter but genuinely useful. Researchers tracked one-point-one million building permits from two thousand to twenty twenty-five and found that approval timelines — not actual construction — drive most of the delay in getting housing built. That's fueling a push for permit shot clocks: mandated deadlines for approvals. This matters for the supply conversation you hear constantly in BC. When people blame builders for slow delivery, the data says the bottleneck is often sitting in the approval process, on the municipal side. It's a helpful, evidence-backed counterpoint to keep in your pocket when housing supply comes up — and it's directly relevant to the affordability pressures shaping your Langley and Vancouver holdings.

Let's come home to Kamloops, where the municipal drama continues. A sitting city councillor is now asking the B.C. Court of Appeal to dismiss the mayor's case. This is an escalation of the legal turmoil at city hall, and the timing is notable — it's unfolding right as the municipal election campaign builds. We've been tracking the field taking shape: Winston jumping into the mayoral race after a decade of deliberation, and now the candidates staking out positions. The through-line for you is that Kamloops is heading into this election with genuine instability at the top, and that backdrop shapes everything from housing policy to how the city presents itself.

Speaking of the campaign, mayoral contender O'Reilly is pitching a consolidated shelter and supportive-housing 'campus' model — the idea being that clustering services would balance community needs against neighbourhood concerns. Homelessness and supportive housing are clearly going to be a defining issue in this race, and how the candidates frame it tells you a lot about where the city's political energy is headed.

And a small bright spot: a new Kamloops elementary school is tracking to come in well below its sixty-five-point-three-million-dollar budget. In a tight fiscal environment, an infrastructure project landing under budget is a genuinely nice piece of news — and a reminder that not everything at the municipal level is conflict and controversy.

Two global items worth your attention as a senior leader. The first is significant for Canada: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed making Canada the EU's first-ever associate member. That's a big idea, floated as Prime Minister Carney is actively courting Europe. If it develops, it signals a meaningful realignment in Canadian trade, security, and — relevant to your higher-ed work — talent and mobility flows. This is early-stage and aspirational, but it's the kind of structural shift that eventually touches immigration frameworks and international education corridors. Worth watching as it evolves.

The second is a landmark accountability ruling: an EU-backed court in The Hague convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci on four counts of war crimes and sentenced him to twenty-five years. It's a major moment in Balkan justice, and part of a broader pattern this week of international courts asserting themselves — Duterte also appeared at the ICC. I mention it mostly for awareness; these are the kinds of developments that shape the global governance climate in the background of everything else.

And one BC public-safety item to close the news. Five gun-control advocacy groups are renewing pressure on the RCMP to disclose details about the firearms used in the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting, arguing that secrecy and accountability can coexist. I'm flagging it because it's a BC story that touches directly on public safety and institutional transparency — the same accountability theme running through today's briefing, just in a much more serious register. It's worth keeping an eye on how the RCMP responds.

So here's what I'd take away today, Midya. The strongest thread is governance — the Axios piece on regulators who don't use the technology they're governing, and the mortgage-file adjudication story, are two different windows onto the same problem you've built your practice around: who's accountable for AI decisions, and do the people signing off actually understand them. Either one could become a strong thought-leadership post this week, and the governance-literacy angle is the sharper of the two. On the client side, the higher-ed divergence is the real signal — graduate enrolment rising while the undergraduate market tightens is a strategy conversation worth initiating, not just noting. And keep half an eye on the EU-Canada proposal; it's early, but structural shifts like that eventually reshape the talent flows your enrollment clients depend on. Have a focused day — I'll catch you tomorrow.

topStories.headline: An aging Congress attempts to regulate AI without using it
topStories.summary: More than two dozen lawmakers and governors told Axios they don't use AI or have rarely touched it, even as pressure to regulate it intensifies — raising the question of whether rule-makers can govern what they don't understand.
topStories.contentAngle: Public-institution AI governance: the credibility gap between regulators and the technology — a framework for how public boards and university leadership should build AI literacy before writing policy.

topStories.headline: AI can read the mortgage file, but who decides which facts are true?
topStories.summary: Conflicting payroll, loan-origination, tax and bank data are forcing lenders to define when AI-surfaced evidence counts as supported versus unresolved — an adjudication problem, not a reading problem.
topStories.contentAngle: AI in real estate operations: the 'source of truth' problem — brokerages and lenders need a governance layer that decides which AI outputs are actionable, not just faster document processing.
